summary:
Pakistan's legal framework for transgender people is progressive on paper and broken in enforcement. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognised self-perceived gender identity, barred discrimination in education, employment and healthcare, and the 2020 Rules added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents. Those protections remain formally in force, but the Federal Shariat Court ruled on 19 May 2023, across 12 shariat petitions, that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act — covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity, and inheritance — do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The UK Home Office country note of November 2025 records the 2023 ruling as leaving ongoing legal disputes over which provisions survive.

Amnesty International called the ruling a blow to the rights of an already beleaguarded group and had warned the Pakistani government on 17 May 2023 against adopting amendments that violate human-rights standards. Justice Project Pakistan's assessment is that the central failure is implementation rather than absence of law: statutory protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment, and its policy brief makes specific recommendations on custody and police safeguards.

Lethal violence against transgender women is continuing and recent. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the largest city, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. In a separate night-time attack reported in February 2026, activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana were fired at through a door with three bullets and narrowly escaped; the same report describes a wave of violence leaving Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out. Estimates cited in 2025 put the transgender citizen population at around 500,000.

Police conduct compounds the risk. Accounts published in October 2025 describe transgender Pakistanis facing street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion and ridicule at police stations, alongside the violence itself. A legislator, Senator Mushtaq Ahmad, has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity, an active retrograde legislative push against the self-identification model.

On sexual conduct, the UK Home Office note of November 2025 states that consensual same-sex acts are criminalised under section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code, carrying two years to life, with the definition unclear and covering male-to-male sex; Human Dignity Trust (December 2024) records only men as criminalised. The same note assesses that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report likewise records section 377 criminalisation, societal violence and discrimination, and notes that transgender people (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition while facing harassment and violence. No trans-traveller-specific entry or screening rules are recorded in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Act was hailed internationally as a legislative turning point for the region, and The Diplomat's July 2025 assessment frames the country's transgender citizens as legally recognised but socially forsaken — statutory rights that do not match lived status. That contrast is the organising fact of the security picture: a visitor encounters a state that formally recognises gender identity while sections of the same statute are under challenge in the religious court system.

The gap is documented by Pakistani domestic media as well as international bodies. The News' October 2025 analysis sets the 2018 affirmation of self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 'X' marker against bullet-riddled bodies on highways and routine refusal of housing, medical care and police cooperation.

For comparison with neighbouring jurisdictions, the country's recognition of self-identified gender and a third administrative marker places it ahead of most of the region in statutory terms, while the 2023 Federal Shariat Court intervention and the proposed gender re-assignment board move in the opposite direction. The violence documented in Karachi over 2024 to 2026 shows the practical risk level regardless of which way the statutory argument runs.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents hold a statutory right to self-perceived gender identity under the 2018 Act, and the 2020 Rules provide a neutral 'X' marker for official documents, giving administrative recognition without a surgical requirement. Inheritance rights secured by the same Act were among the provisions struck down by the Federal Shariat Court in May 2023.

Discrimination in education, employment and healthcare is prohibited by statute, but residents report dismissal at hospitals, rejection by landlords and employment barriers in practice. Police stations are described as places of suspicion and ridicule rather than protection, and Justice Project Pakistan documents torture and ill-treatment in custody as an implementation failure of the existing law.

The estimated transgender population is around 500,000 citizens facing social exclusion and abuse. The community's most visible activists have been targeted directly: Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana survived a shooting in which three bullets were fired through a door. A proposal by Senator Mushtaq Ahmad for a government gender re-assignment board would place control of official gender identity in state hands and would narrow the current self-identification model if adopted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of section 377 remains unresolved in the sources: the UK Home Office note calls the definition unclear, and Human Dignity Trust records that only men fall within the offence. Whether the provision would be applied against a transgender visitor, as opposed to cisgender men, is not sourced.

Which sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 remain operative after the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 ruling is subject to ongoing legal disputes per the November 2025 UK Home Office note; the sources do not establish the final legislative or appellate position on sections 2(f), 3 and 7.

No source in this inventory addresses visa conditions, airport or border screening, gender-marker checks at entry, or detention conditions specific to foreign transgender visitors. Nothing is recorded here about prison or immigration-detention placement policy for trans detainees, nor about the availability of hormone treatment or trans-related healthcare for short-term visitors.
